concept.name: Physical settlement
concept.definition: A provision in a futures or other derivative contract requiring delivery of the actual underlying commodity or asset (or a delivery instrument such as a warehouse receipt) to satisfy the contract at maturity.
concept.intuition: With physical settlement, holding the contract to the end means real goods or securities change hands — not just a check for the price difference.
concept.mechanics: After the last trading day, remaining shorts tender delivery notices through the clearing organization, and remaining longs must accept delivery and pay the invoice price (e.g., for bond futures, invoice price = contract size x futures settlement price x conversion factor + accrued interest). Delivery occurs at exchange-approved facilities during the delivery period.
concept.failure_modes: Traders who fail to close longs before first notice day can be obligated to take (and pay for) full physical delivery, including storage, transport, and financing; squeezes on deliverable supply can distort prices near expiry.
concept.misconceptions: Most futures positions never reach delivery — they are offset beforehand — but physical settlement is not merely theoretical: the deliverability of the contract is what ties the futures price to the cash market at expiry (convergence).
concept.example: A refiner holding CME WTI crude futures through expiry receives delivery notices for 1,000-barrel lots at the Cushing, Oklahoma delivery point and pays the invoice price per contract.

citations.source: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
